challenges.name: debounced-search-quiz
challenges.title: Stale responses and fake timers
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from the search incident: a slow response that arrived last, and a test that checks a 300 ms debounce in a few milliseconds.

questions.explanation: True. When query changes, React runs the previous effect's cleanup before the next effect. Aborting there rejects the pending fetch for "re" with an AbortError, so its .then(setResults) never runs, whenever its bytes arrive. The fetch for "react" belongs to the last effect and is the only one allowed to set state. Abort does not stop the server from doing the work, and you still want a debounce so that four of these five requests are never sent; but for correctness the cleanup alone is enough. Verify it in the Network panel: the superseded requests show as (canceled). The misconception is that the order of responses follows the order of requests.

False. Fake timers replace setTimeout with a clock the test moves by hand, so time in the code under test is exactly the time the test advances: at 299 ms the timer has not fired, at 300 ms it has. That pins the boundary to the millisecond, deterministically, which a real 300 ms wait cannot do (a slow CI machine fires late, and the test cannot tell 299 from 320). What fake timers do not prove is how the real browser schedules timers, which is not what this test is about. The misconception is that a test about time has to spend real time.

challenges.name: debounced-search
challenges.title: Debounced search that cancels stale requests
challenges.description: Typing "react hooks" quickly in the catalog search box sent 11 requests, and the slow response for "re" arrived last and replaced the right results. Write createDebouncedSearch({ clock, debounceMs, search, show, showError }), which returns { onInput(text), dispose() }. Rules: (1) Every onInput cancels the pending timer, if any. (2) If text.trim() is empty: do not send anything, abort the in-flight request if there is one, and call show([]) at once. (3) Otherwise start a timer with clock.setTimeout for debounceMs; when it fires, abort the previous in-flight request (if any) first, then call search(text.trim(), signal) with the signal of a new FakeAbortController. (4) Only the latest request may update the screen: when it resolves, call show(results); when it rejects with an error whose name is not "AbortError", call showError(error.message). A request stops being the latest as soon as a newer request is sent, the box is cleared (rule 2) or dispose is called; its later response or error is ignored, even when the server ignored the abort and answered anyway. An earlier response that arrives while a new timer is still pending is still the latest, so it is shown. (5) dispose() (the component unmounts) cancels the pending timer and aborts the in-flight request; nothing is shown afterwards. Use only the injected clock (no setTimeout, no Date). The runner replays a timeline - { "input": text }, { "type": chars, "every": ms }, { "advance": ms }, { "unmount": true } - against a fake API with per-query latencies, some queries that ignore abort and some that fail with HTTP 503, runs the clock 10 more seconds at the end, and prints the event log: requests, aborts, responses, what was shown and errors, each with its time.
hints: Three separate jobs hide in this box: deciding when to send (the timer), stopping the network work that is no longer needed (abort), and deciding whether an answer may still reach the screen. Which of the three protects you when the server ignores the abort?

Keep three variables in the closure returned by createDebouncedSearch: the pending timer id, the controller of the in-flight request, and a counter or id of the latest request. Look at what each of onInput, the timer callback, the .then handlers and dispose has to read or change; the handlers compare the id they captured with the current latest one.

A similar pattern on a different feature, autosave of a lesson note with a 1 s delay: onChange clears the pending timer and starts a new one; when it fires, saveCount += 1 and the save captures const mine = saveCount; when its response arrives, it updates the "Saved" label only if mine === saveCount, so an older save that finishes late never overwrites the status of a newer one.
